content.thinking:
The repo seems to be the full sample set, so I should avoid opening unrelated files. Baking geometry without UVs should be fine since baker zeroes them out, and flat non-indexed geometry should work with b.part. Now I'm writing the sample code, starting with a helper function for generating keys.

Writing imports and palette constants...

Writing tail paint logic...

That resolve call stays inside the try block, so the current context is preserved correctly even when the returned paint is unresolved. Now I'm working out the leg paint definition, blending rust-brown fur fading to dark using a position-based fur edge function.

I'm deciding the paint constants need to live inside build() since they depend on TOP, which is only known after the rock geometry is constructed, even though paint functions themselves are pure and could technically sit at module scope. Now I'm writing the skull paint function, defining an elliptical brow spot region using offset coordinates and ellipse inequality checks.

Working out eye decal placement...

Adjusting the brow spot to y=+0.036 with radii 0.011x/0.007y, confirming the surface height comes out to about 0.031 there. Now I'm thinking about the tear mark streak red pandas have running from the inner eye corner down toward the mouth over the white cheek fur, needing to place this separately from the eye decal—on the cheek sphere it'd run from roughly (±0.03,-0.02) to (±0.036,-0.05), while on the skull paint layer it'd occupy a region below the eye around x 0.025-0.04, y -0.04 to -0.015, with a rust-dark tear color.

I'm checking whether the cream-colored cheek spheres would accidentally cover up the tear mark painted on the skull, running through the geometry to see where the cheek surface extends past the skull surface at the tear's location—finding that with the current cheek placement it does cover the mark, so I need to shift the cheek centers further outward and shrink their radius so the tear streak stays visible underneath.

Now I'm sketching the overall head placement relative to the body: setting a top plateau height, deriving the body's y0 origin, then stacking chest, neck base, and head base positions forward along z, and placing the skull center and radius so the muzzle extends out front while checking that the neck base doesn't awkwardly poke through the head or chest.

Then I shift to defining body radii along the spine as a function of path position t, using a piecewise set of keyframes from hips to neck to taper the torso naturally, with rounded caps at both ends so the body blends smoothly into the head and hides at the hips.

For the legs, I use the same ellipse radius function shape, positioned at shoulder joints offset ±0.06 in x. Then for the neck collar, I'm working out where to place the cutting plane for the loop—trying to avoid it falling at the chest/shoulder joint where leg loops already intersect, and instead positioning it near the neckBase joint further forward along z.

I settle on cutting the collar loop at z=0.195 with a tilt following the tangent there, where the neck radius is about 0.058, giving enough clearance from the skull sphere so the collar doesn't collide with the head. For the bell ornament, I'm figuring out that it should hang from the lowest point of the collar loop path (roughly the midpoint parameter going around), placed slightly below and forward of that point as a small gold sphere, inheriting bone weights from the path so it follows the neck naturally.

Then I'm deciding on the overall ornament layout: a central gem pendant on a gold frame hanging just below the collar over the chest, flanked by two small gold bells offset slightly to either side rather than clustered together, plus a teal tassel dangling beneath the pendant with a gold cap and bead detail.

I'll use the skin's nearest-point function to keep pendant positions on the surface. For the gold filigree, I'm reconsidering placement—too small for the pendant itself, so I'll put the swirl decal on the flat collar band trim instead.

I'm adding gold trim sweeps above and below the collar band, plus small gold beads distributed along the collar path, and planning a similar looped band around the tail joint with gold edges and beads instead of a tassel. For the ear, I'm sketching an asymmetric gold ring cuff on just the left ear base with a tiny hanging teal tassel and gem, now defining the outline points for the ear geometry.

Still choosing ear colors...

Now I'm planning the ear geometry: outer ears in deep rust with an inner cream layer scaled down and offset forward, plus fluffy cream tufts rooted along the inner ear base using oriented card frames.

I'm also setting up cheek ruff cards, scattering cream tuft shapes across the cheek surface with directional leaning and a teardrop texture with soft cream tones and a subtle shadow line.

Now adding the eyes (using the anime eye decal with built-in shine), whiskers as three thin cream rods per side emerging from the muzzle, a dark nose sphere with a small highlight, and a lower jaw ellipsoid with a cream chin for the mouth.

Skipping teeth and tongue since the mouth stays closed. I'm now setting up the rock surface part as a flat-shaded bone attached to the root joint, and planning a faceted stone paint shader with cel shading for crisp Genshin-style rock shadows.

Writing stone paint shader...

I'll need to import the cells function for the crack pattern, and add a darker tint near the bottom edge to suggest dirt. For moss, I'm thinking of scattering flattened spheres on the top plateau to create natural-looking moss pads.

I'll use flat colored strings MOSS, MOSS_HI, MOSS_DK with flat shading for that cel-faceted look, placing the moss mound where the panda's paws stand. Now I'm defining SVG texture strings for details like the cream tuft pattern.

Writing texture SVGs...

Decorating the mossy stone with a carved gold-trimmed dendro rune panel, using a non-glowing gold filigree ring decal layered slightly above a glowing green rune decal for depth.

I'm figuring out where on the rock's lower front face to project the decal, accounting for the faceted surface normal and the panda's legs blocking part of the view, then starting to code the build function.

Setting up the root joint, rock part, and a surface ray-cast to find the top height for positioning, then planning the spine chain hierarchy starting from root.

Still working out the joint hierarchy...

Now I'm sketching the body sweep using the spine and neck as the bone path with a defined radius function and color, then starting to set up the leg generation loop for both sides symmetrically.

Working out the fore limb joint positions...

That distance checks out roughly, giving a mild bend with the elbow back. I'm now setting up the leg chain to parent off the chest point with named joints and a contact point at the toe, and considering whether to build it as a straight polyline versus a smoothed curve through the points—keeping it as a polyline preserves sharp joint corners better than rounding through catmull interpolation.

For sweeping the foreleg, I'm defining a radius profile that tapers from shoulder to paw, flattening the foot segment into an oval cross-section rather than circular. Then for the paw itself, I'm planning three toes positioned relative to the toe center point.

Writing toe chains and claws...

Now thinking about color: red panda feet are blackish, darker at the paw bottom with rust fur above. For hind legs I'm placing the hip and toe positions with appropriate segment lengths, keeping the sole forward and angling the knee forward slightly.

Checking the geometry: the heel sits behind the hip in z, and with thigh and shin lengths totaling about 0.185 against a vertical drop of roughly 0.137, there's a noticeable bend with the knee pushed forward and the shin angling back to the heel -- the thigh is mostly buried in the body, which is fine. I'm bumping up the thigh radius for a thicker hind leg shape.

Now I'm building the tail curve using a sequence of control points that arc upward and outward from the body.

The tail chains off the first spine joint at the hips, with one joint per curve segment (tail1 through tail5), swept with a radius profile. Total tail length comes to about .47, which is reasonable, and I'm giving it a bushy taper -- narrow at the root, widening toward the middle, then tapering to a rounded tip. I need to lower the tail's final height since the original rise puts it taller than the ears, so I'm adjusting the y-values down to keep it more proportional.

I'm also planning small fur tuft cards scattered across the flanks and belly, with their color tinted by sampling the body's coat paint at each card's root so the tufts pick up the rust coloring naturally.

I'm separating the rust tufts (around 60 cards on shoulders, thighs, and chest) from a darker tuft texture for the chest and legs. For scene dressing, I'm scattering grass cards on the rock plateau using a filter that targets upward-facing, elevated surfaces, while adding a keep-out zone near the panda's feet so the grass blades don't poke through the paws and legs.

I'm adding moss pads with similar rules, a fringe of around 70 low grass/ferns at the base, a few scattered flowers, and three mushrooms placed at the rear right of the base, all kept within the floor and height limits.

Now I'm working out a hanging vine on the left edge of the rock — finding an anchor point near the top edge, then draping a rough catmull-rom path down the surface with a slight lift so it follows the rock contour, using a thin sweep radius and a green vine color.

I'm placing leaf cards along the vine path using frame-based orientation so they lean outward from the tangent direction, adjusting lean and flow parameters to make them stick out naturally rather than lying flat.

Writing dendro mote placement...

I'm making sure the sparkle star cards face the camera correctly by setting flow to the z-axis so the card front looks along that direction, and adding cross:true so they're visible from multiple angles — about 8 sparkles with double-sided faces should give good coverage without adding too many parts. I'll keep rune decals and gold accents minimal to control part count, maybe skipping the extra floating leaf idea to stay efficient.

For the panda's accessories, I'll stick with the ear cuff, tail band, and collar rather than adding a forehead leaf mark, with a glowing glyph on the pendant as a small extra detail.

Now I'm writing the rock geometry function, which starts from an icosahedron, filters out triangles below a height threshold to carve out a flatter base, and reconstructs a non-indexed buffer geometry with computed normals for that faceted rock look.

I'm settling on a higher subdivision detail level (3) for the icosphere to get a smoother, more faceted silhouette with around 160 triangles in the upper half, then defining a layered noise function combining multiple sine waves to displace the vertices into an irregular lumpy rock shape, with the top vertices flattened and shaped differently from the sides.

I notice the top plateau region (where y≥0.74) ends up perfectly flat at a fixed height, which looks too artificial, so I'm adding a small secondary bump pattern on top to break up the uniformity while keeping the overall flattened cap.

Now I'm moving on to writing the actual file: setting up a head connector point offset from the body path, attaching parts to the head bone, and defining a reusable ellipsoid helper built from a scaled sphere geometry so I can shape cheeks, eyes, and other facial features consistently.

For eyes specifically, I'm computing a hit point on the skull surface using azimuth/elevation angles mirrored for left/right, then placing a decal there sized appropriately, tweaking the dimensions slightly larger for visibility and bumping up the skull's sphere subdivisions so the decal conforms smoothly. For ears, I'm working out the outward-facing axis vectors per side to orient the ear shape correctly relative to the head.

Still working out the cross product...

Now I'm sketching the ear outline coordinates, aiming for a broad base with a rounded triangular shape pointing up and outward, like a red panda's ear.

I'm working out the layering: giving the ear thickness with a beveled edge, then creating an inner scaled-down shape offset inward, and setting up a paint function that darkens the tip while keeping the base rust-colored.

I'm defining the ear's outer coloring as dark blackish-brown near the tip fading to deep rust at the base, with a cream inner lining, and setting up a hinge joint for the ear's attachment to the head. I'm also placing small fur tufts along the inner ear base, angling their frames outward so they lean naturally.

For the ear tufts I'm tuning the standing orientation and lean angle so they flow outward realistically, and attaching them to the ear's bone for rigging. I'm scattering additional cheek fur cards with filtered placement based on surface normals, giving them a backward-and-outward flow with a steep lean, and deciding to skip a forehead stripe for now before moving into the actual write-up.

Now I'm defining the tail band and collar loop surfaces, attaching a sweep along the tail and a closed-loop sweep around the neck for the collar, working out how the sideways and normal radii translate into band width and thickness so the collar ribbon ends up roughly 2.2cm wide and 0.8cm thick with the right lift offset.

For the gold trim rings, I'm planning two loops offset along the neck axis on either side of the collar path, making sure to explicitly pass the neck axis as the direction since the default would wrongly use world-up for a literal point. I still need to place bells, the pendant gem, and nail down the exact collar frame location at the neck's second joint position.

Checking the neck loop radius and position against the skull and shoulder geometry to confirm nothing overlaps incorrectly — the neck cut sits cleanly between the head and shoulders. Now I'm writing the grass blade shapes as SVG paths...

Still writing SVG paths...

I'm sketching out the flower with rotated petal ellipses, a gold center, and a thin stem, then moving on to defining the leaf shape in its own viewBox.

Designing fern, sparkle, filigree ring, and rune icons...

Now I'm working out decal projection onto faceted rock surfaces, and setting up flat-shaded icosahedron pebbles scattered with slight rotation and scale variation.

With no rotation, the icosahedron's max y is about 0.85r, so scaling by 0.6 and setting center at roughly 0.5r keeps the bottom just under the surface, around -0.01.

Now I'm sketching the rock geometry as a flat-shaded part attached to the root bone, and thinking through the lathe profile for a mushroom cap -- a half-silhouette from the axis outward and back to form a closed cap shape.

For the mushrooms I'm choosing a teal glowing cap color with cream spots, and cream rod-shaped stems, placing a cluster of three on the back right edge of the rock using angular offsets around its surface. Setting up a helper function to compute spawn positions on the rock's surface by azimuth and elevation.

Now I'm figuring out ground-based coordinates for mushroom placement near the plateau edge, picking small x/z offsets like (-0.17,-0.2) and (-0.13,-0.27) so they sit naturally on the sloped terrain without overlapping each other.

For moss, I'm scattering flattened sphere pads onto surfaces with upward-facing normals, embedding them slightly into the rock while keeping a clearance radius around each foot position so the moss doesn't collide with the toes and heels. I'm listing out the front and hind foot coordinates to build that keep-out check, then moving on to placing the pendant.

The pendant sits at the bottom of a collar loop traced around the neck's lower joint, with the gem hanging slightly below and forward of that point. I'm checking whether this position falls within the visible front region of the chest given the chest's radius and z-extent so the pendant doesn't get buried inside the body geometry.

Writing torus and gem code...

I also need to add a tassel hanging from the gem's bottom with spike shapes, and make sure bone assignment picks the nearest neck joint explicitly rather than relying on auto-detection. I'll import the OutlinePoint type for typed outline arrays before writing the actual part-list code.

For the fur edge detail on the face, I'm computing a scalloped cream mask using a zigzag pattern along the crown — but I realize the edge level might cross into the eye region, so I need to adjust it so the cream patch sits correctly around the muzzle and cheeks rather than cutting through the eyes, matching a red panda's facial markings.

I'll also add a dark eye-ring patch (dark brown ellipse) around each eye position, visible as a thin ring where the decal doesn't fully cover it, consistent with the red panda's natural dark eye markings. Then I'll move on to finalizing the write-up.

input.command: mkdir -p scratch/redPandaSonnet; ls samples | head -3; sed -n 1,60p scripts/typecheck.ts | head -40
